claims.text: High-temperature sliding wear causes FeNiCrCoCu coatings to develop an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous near-surface layer.
The refined near-surface layer promotes inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
Inverse Hall-Petch behavior associated with the refined surface layer reduces friction and wear.
The baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating has a standard microcrystalline grain structure.
FeNiCrCoCu coatings should be tested at 200–400 °C under high contact loads and compared with room-temperature tests.
Oxidation must be minimal or controlled for dynamic grain refinement to remain the dominant wear mechanism.
The structural mediator is an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous layer in the deformed near-surface region.
Elevated temperature coupled with sustained shear stress drives dynamic amorphization and grain refinement at the FeNiCrCoCu surface.
Dynamic surface refinement reduces effective shear strength through an inverse Hall-Petch effect.
The transformed surface enhances grain-boundary sliding and local superplasticity.
Formation of the transformed surface lowers friction and wear.
High-temperature testing should produce a TEM- or EBSD-detectable ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous sublayer.
High-temperature-tested coatings should have lower friction coefficients than room-temperature-tested coatings.
High-temperature-tested coatings should have lower wear rates than room-temperature-tested coatings.
Dynamic microstructural changes are minimal in FeNiCrCoCu during room-temperature wear.
Room-temperature wear of FeNiCrCoCu follows conventional wear mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism operates approximately within 200–400 °C and at high loads typical of protective coatings.
At substantially higher temperatures or under aggressive oxidation, other degradation processes may dominate.
Differences between FeNiCrCoCu and CoCrFeMnNi make the transformation thresholds and magnitude of wear reduction uncertain.
Failure to form the refined layer or failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear would falsify the hypothesis.
